Jobs with the same title, File Clerk, vary considerably: government case files and licensing records, client files at law and accounting firms, medical records and follow-up information at hospitals and clinics, student records at schools, and corporate contracts and personnel records. They differ in record types, special retention and confidentiality requirements, exposure to personal information or restricted materials, use of paper or electronic systems, electronic records and scanning duties, and any additional reception or financial support duties. Before comparing jobs, check the types and sensitivity of records, specific retention and destruction requirements, filing and document systems, retrieval and checkout/return procedures, access to personal information, and local personal information protection and records management requirements.

Test this through a paper exercise: given an entirely fictional filing assignment specifying record types and quantities, filing rules and numbering methods, retention and confidentiality requirements, available storage containers and systems, and inquiry scenarios, write a classification and numbering plan, filing and registration procedures, methods for recording retrieval and checkout/return, criteria for removing records and handling them at the end of their retention period, situations requiring supervisor confirmation, and key confidentiality and authorized access considerations.

Signals worth considering: willingness to check each document's number and location against the rules, sustain attention to detail and accurately record checkouts and returns, handle restricted materials cautiously, and provide service within authorization. Signals calling for caution: filing from memory without checking numbers, treating retention and destruction rules as negotiable, and giving insufficient attention to access controls for personal information and restricted materials.

First consider whether you are willing to do detailed, clearly prescribed, predominantly seated document processing over the long term and follow retention and confidentiality requirements. Test this with this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

File clerks' daily work follows a cycle of receiving, classifying, filing, retrieving, and maintaining records: collect materials that departments or colleagues need filed; scan or read incoming materials to determine their classification and filing location; sort and classify them by content, purpose, user criteria, or chronological, alphabetical, or numerical order; number or code materials and register them in an index; place them in filing cabinets, file boxes, drawers, or electronic systems; record filing and retrieval activity and generate reports; locate, copy, and deliver information to authorized users on request and track checked-out files for return; remove outdated or unnecessary materials under filing maintenance rules or legal requirements, destroying them or transferring them to inactive storage; periodically check placement, legibility, and condition; enter file numbers and updates into the system; answer inquiries about records or files; and, when necessary, improve or implement new filing systems and design related forms. O*NET also lists general office activities and some general financial support. Check the job description for additional duties; do not exclude all financial or system improvement activities.

Work context | File clerks work in offices, records rooms, and service counters, following a daily cycle of receiving and classifying, numbering and indexing, filing and storage, retrieval and checkout/return, recording and reporting, and removal and maintenance.
Workplaces | Government records rooms and service counters; law and accounting firms; hospital and clinic records departments; school records offices; corporate administration and human resources departments; outsourced records service providers.
Working conditions | Predominantly seated work and repetitive clerical tasks (in O*NET work context responses, 52% sit continually or almost continually, and 32% perform repetitive motions continually or almost continually); schedules are primarily regular (97%); 66% of respondents work 40 hours per week and 30% work more than 40 hours; precision and accuracy are highly important (48% extremely important, 38% very important); 34% face strict deadlines daily and 56% at least weekly; 70% have constant contact with others; 51% describe the job as not at all automated and 21% as highly automated.
Main work objects | Paper documents and case files, licenses and supporting documents, electronic documents and scans, numbers and indexes, storage containers and filing cabinets, document management and database systems, and checkout/return and destruction records.
Collaboration | Colleagues and departmental contacts, supervisors or records managers, information and confidentiality officers, external inquirers, and system and records service providers.
Tools and materials | Filing cabinets and storage containers, coding and binding supplies, scanning and copying equipment, document management and database systems, spreadsheet and word processing software, filing rules, and retention schedules.
Applicable requirements | Records management and retention requirements, personal information protection and confidentiality requirements, authorized access controls for restricted materials, lawful destruction and transfer procedures, information security and account permission requirements, and employment, wage, and working time rules.
Recordkeeping requirements | Filing and retrieval logs, checkout/return records, index and numbering change records, retention and destruction approvals, and system operation and permission change records must be retained under employer procedures.
Safety and jurisdictional boundaries | Personal information protection and confidentiality, authorized access to restricted materials, records retention and lawful destruction, and information security and permissions must follow records management procedures, personal information protection requirements, and competent authorities' rules. entries.question: What do file clerks mainly do?

entries.answer: Responsibilities differ: file clerks focus on filing documents, numbering and indexing, recording retrievals, and removal and maintenance; document management specialists design and implement document management policies, processes, and systems; archivists appraise, arrange, and preserve records of long-term value; receptionists and information clerks primarily receive visitors and answer general inquiries; data entry keyers primarily enter data in bulk; bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks primarily process and reconcile accounts; administrative services managers organize administrative and records work and manage staff; and library assistants, clerical, primarily handle circulation and arrangement of library materials.
entries.question: How does this differ from document management specialists and archivists?

entries.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1–2 (very little to some preparation), with SVP below 6.0. In its education survey, approximately 38% reported an associate degree or other two-year qualification, 30% a high school diploma or equivalent, and 23% some college without a degree. BLS states that the occupation typically requires a high school diploma and learning on the job; some employers may prefer candidates with some college or an associate degree. Roles involving personal information and restricted materials typically also require confidentiality commitments and permission management training; destruction approvals must follow records management procedures. In mainland China, common requirements are education related to secretarial studies, archives, or information management plus job training, subject to recruitment announcements and local rules.
entries.question: What education and qualifications are needed?

entries.answer: A more precise assessment is that systems and tools will continue taking over classification, indexing, and retrieval tasks, while the occupation mainly undergoes a shift toward higher-level responsibilities and structural adjustment. The ILO's 2023 study shows clerical tasks have the highest exposure to generative AI. However, people must still bear responsibility under procedures for authorized access, confidentiality judgments, retention and destruction, exceptional retrievals, and user responses. The conclusion is therefore changing work methods and responsibility priorities rather than wholesale replacement.
entries.question: Will AI replace this occupation?

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of workers' wage distribution within the same statistical period, not a starting wage. This occupation mainly has regular schedules and most jobs are full-time, with some requiring overtime at month-end, quarter-end, and year-end. Individual income depends on institution type, job level, and actual hours (O*NET work context shows that 66% of respondents work 40 hours per week and 30% work more than 40 hours).

entries.answer: Yes. BLS states that this occupation typically requires a high school diploma and learning on the job, with most roles learned through guidance. Roles involving personal information and restricted materials typically require confidentiality commitments and permission management training. Disclosure, retention periods, and destruction must follow records management procedures and personal information protection requirements. Feasibility depends on the target employer and local rules. details: For checking tasks, work activities, work context, technology skills, interest code (C), and preparation level (Job Zone 1–2).

Main tasks include general office work; recording filing and retrieval and generating reports; collecting materials to be filed; locating, copying, and delivering information to authorized users; adding or creating records; sorting and classifying under rules; reading incoming materials to determine filing locations; removing outdated materials under rules or legal requirements; answering record inquiries; numbering, coding, and indexing; placing materials in storage containers; improving filing systems; entering data; handling general financial matters; tracking checked-out files; conducting periodic checks; retrieving microform materials; and operating mechanized filing cabinets.

Work context: 97% have regular schedules; 66% work 40 hours per week and 30% more than 40 hours; 52% sit continually or almost continually, and 32% perform repetitive motions continually or almost continually; precision and accuracy are extremely important to 48% and very important to 38%; 34% face strict deadlines daily and 56% at least weekly; 70% have constant contact with others; 51% describe work as not at all automated and 21% as highly automated.

O*NET's national wage page (onetonline.org/link/localwages/43-4071.00) gives this occupation's national percentiles: annual wages of USD 31,200 at 10%, USD 36,420 at 25%, USD 43,600 at the median, USD 51,770 at 75%, and USD 63,490 at 90%; corresponding hourly wages are USD 15.00, 17.51, 20.96, 24.89, and 30.53.

Employment is projected to decline by 2% over 2025—2035 (approximately -30,100 workers). Despite the decline, approximately 125,600 job openings are projected annually over the decade, all from replacing workers who leave their jobs or exit the labor force.

Typical entry education is a high school diploma followed by learning on the job, with no related work experience required. Information clerks work in nearly every industry, with many in government, hotels, and medical facilities; most work full-time.

subject.name: File Clerks
subject.summary: File correspondence, cards, invoices, receipts, and other records alphabetically, numerically, or according to the organization's filing system, and locate and retrieve materials on request: scan or read incoming materials to determine their classification and filing location; sort and classify them by content, purpose, user criteria, or chronological, alphabetical, or numerical order; number or code materials and register them in an index; place materials in filing cabinets, file boxes, drawers, or other storage containers; record filing and retrieval activity and generate electronic reports; locate, copy, and deliver information to authorized users on request; collect materials that departments or colleagues need filed; remove outdated or unnecessary materials under filing maintenance rules or legal requirements, destroying them or transferring them to inactive storage; periodically check file placement, legibility, and condition; enter data such as file numbers, updates, or file information codes into the system; answer inquiries about records or files; and improve or implement new filing systems.
